title: Invitations — can, may, must, and how to say no
goal: Invite, accept and decline politely — while sorting out the words that English squeezes into "can" and "may", and meeting one word that never changes form at all: *lahko*.
bekal: accepting and declining invitations without sounding rude

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Vabilo k Maji domov
dialogs.intro: Thursday lunchtime. Maja invites Budi to dinner at her family's home — and explains a word that never changes.

lines.speaker: Maja:
lines.text: Bi prišel v soboto na večerjo?
lines.id: Would you like to come for dinner on Saturday?
lines.literal: would come-m on Saturday to dinner?

lines.speaker: Maja:
lines.id: No need. You can bring some wine.

lines.speaker: Maja:
lines.id: "Lahko" isn't a verb. It's an adverb.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Torej lahko grem, lahko greš, lahko gremo.
lines.literal: so can I-go, can you-go, can we-go.

lines.speaker: Maja:
lines.text: Tako je. Samo glagol se spreminja.
lines.id: That's right. Only the verb changes.
lines.literal: so is. only verb self changes.

lines.speaker: Maja:
lines.text: Super. Ne pozabi na rože za mamo!
lines.id: Great. Don't forget flowers for Mom!
lines.literal: great. not forget-imp on flower-pl for mom-acc!

notes: **Lahko never changes form.** It's not a verb but an adverb, and the verb after it is what changes: *lahko grem*, *lahko greš*, *lahko gremo*, *lahko sta prišla*. English speakers often try to bend it like *can/could* — in Slovenian there's nothing to bend.

**Bi prišel? is a polite invitation.** The *bi* form softens everything — it's like "would you like to" rather than "are you coming". The ending follows the gender of the person invited: *Bi prišel?* to a man, *Bi prišla?* to a woman, *Bi prišla?* to two people, *Bi prišli?* to a group or politely.

**Ni treba = no need.** A sentence with no subject, like the weather sentences in unit 16. Its relatives: *Treba je* (it's necessary), *Ni mogoče* (it's not possible), *Ni problema* (no problem). They stay the same no matter who's speaking.

**K nam domov — two direction words at once.** *K nam* means "to our place" and *domov* means "home". Together they mean "to our home". *K* takes the dative from unit 15 and is used for going **to someone's place**.

**Ne pozabi na rože.** The flowers aren't just a pleasantry: in Slovenia, a guest invited to dinner brings something — flowers for the hostess, a bottle of wine, or a cake. Turning up empty-handed isn't fatal, but it's noticed straight away. And flowers always come in odd numbers; even numbers are for funerals.

grammars.title: Lahko, moram, smem, znam — four kinds of "can"
body: English uses "can" and "may" for four things that Slovenian keeps sharply apart. Choosing wrong here won't make you incomprehensible, but it can make you mean something else.

head: Word
Meaning
Changes?
Example
rows: *Tu ne smem kaditi.* — I'm not allowed to smoke here.

after: The difference most often mixed up is between **ne morem**, **ne smem** and **ne znam**. *Ne morem plavati* = I can't swim right now (broken leg, water too cold). *Ne smem plavati* = I'm not allowed to swim. *Ne znam plavati* = I can't swim, I never learned.

*Lahko* is also used for polite requests, and that's the use you'll need most: *Lahko dobim račun?* (could I have the bill?), *Lahko ponovite?* (could you repeat that?), *Lahko pomagam?* (can I help?).

grammars.title: Velelnik — commands
body: Three endings for three numbers, just like the rest of Slovenian. The polite form uses the plural, as usual.
after: To forbid something, put *ne* in front: *Ne pozabi!* (don't forget), *Ne skrbi!* (don't worry), *Ne hodi tja!* (don't go there). Note that negative commands use the **imperfective** verb, not the perfective — so *Ne odpiraj!* (don't open it), not *Ne odpri!*

Slovenian commands sound much friendlier than English speakers expect, especially with *prosim* added: *Počakajte, prosim* (wait a moment, please). They're used in shops, offices and among friends without sounding bossy.

blocks.text: Saying no politely is a skill rarely taught, yet it's one you need most often. The rows at the bottom of this table all decline without closing the door.

head: Slovenščina
Say it
English
rows: I'd like to invite you to dinner.

blocks.text: *Ta teden ne gre* is literally "this week it doesn't go" — a very Slovenian way of declining: no reason given, no over-apologizing, and the door left open. Combined with *Mogoče drugič?*, it turns someone down completely and warmly in two short sentences.

Notice **žal** — a word you met in unit 15 as *Žal mi je*. At the start of a sentence it means "unfortunately" and signals right away that a refusal is coming. Slovenians use it as often as English speakers say "I'm afraid".
If your invitation is accepted, these customs will save you some awkwardness.

blocks.title: Before you go in
items: **Shoes come off.** Almost always, in almost every home. The host will offer you *copate* (house slippers); accept them.
**Bring something.** An odd number of flowers, a bottle of wine, or a cake. If there are small children, something sweet is always right.
**Arrive five to ten minutes after the stated time.** Unlike business appointments, which must be punctual, a dinner invitation gives the host a little leeway.

head: Sentence
Say it
When to use
rows: Shall I take my shoes off?
A toast — look them in the eye

blocks.text: A Slovenian host will offer more food again and again, and one refusal isn't taken as final. If you're really full, *Res sem sit, hvala* with a smile is a clear way to say so without giving offense.

And one custom worth knowing: **when you toast, look the person in the eye**, not at the glass, and say their name if you remember it. Looking at the glass is considered insincere. It's an unwritten rule taken seriously across Central Europe, and following it just once will be noticed.
